findings.confusion: The code returns {"message": "Hello World"}, but the page says the browser shows "Hello FastAPI". Alex would wonder whether the code was copied wrong or something is misconfigured.
findings.suggestion: Make the expected output match the code: {"message": "Hello World"}.

findings.confusion: The page never says to save the code as main.py, and never says how to install FastAPI (for example uv add "fastapi[standard]"). The output mentions main.py, but Alex has to guess the filename and may not have the fastapi command at all.
findings.suggestion: Add a line saying to save the code as main.py and a short install step before running the server.

findings.section: Step 4: define the path operation function
findings.quote: In this case, it is an async function. You could also define it as a normal function instead of async def
findings.confusion: Alex does not know async/await. The page does not say what async means or when to choose one over the other. It is a mild worry, though, because Alex can copy the example as written.
findings.suggestion: Add a one-line note that async can be ignored for now and that either form works, with a link to the async explainer.

findings.quote: FastAPI generates a "schema" with all your API using the OpenAPI standard
findings.confusion: A long run of schema, OpenAPI and JSON Schema definitions comes before Alex has seen the app work. Alex would likely skim it and may not see how it relates to the goal of building an API.
findings.suggestion: Mark the OpenAPI section as optional background, or move it after the recap.

summary: Alex can run the example and finish the page. The mismatched expected output (Hello FastAPI vs Hello World) and the missing save-as-main.py and install steps would cause hesitation and guessing. The async mention and the long OpenAPI digression are minor friction.
